events.title: FOMC Member Bowman Speaks
notes: Given strong productivity gains in recent years, wage growth at this pace is in line with or even below the pace we would expect if inflation was running at 2 percent.

Today's consumer price index suggests that 12-month core PCE inflation likely moved up further to 3.3 percent in October, as upward pressures from higher energy prices and AI-related demand continue to flow through to core goods and services prices.

Economic Outlook and Risks Looking ahead, my expectation is that policies designed to boost the economic potential of the U.S. economy would continue to support productivity, growth, and business confidence.
Monetary policy cannot address that transition directly, but it should support a dynamic labor market that facilitates the necessary retraining and mobility of workers across jobs.
At each FOMC meeting, my colleagues and I will evaluate incoming data, the evolving outlook, and the implications for the risks to our dual-mandate goals of maximum employment and price stability.

noteSrc.title: Bowman, The U.S. Economy and Considerations for Monetary Policy

events.title: FOMC Member Waller Speaks
notes: But inflation remains too high, so I will explain why I believe further tightening of monetary policy will be needed, sooner rather than later, to return inflation to a path that will reach 2 percent in the medium term.
The outline of my speech is to first explain why I voted to hold the policy rate steady at the most recent meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC).
If, however, the hikes are not carried out, markets will reduce expectations of rate hikes and rates will immediately fall, which would loosen monetary policy in an undesirable way.

But I worry that today's labor market dynamism may be low due to impediments to mobility that are affecting long-term and youth unemployment, and this may lead to a less-efficient distribution of workers across jobs, hindering productivity growth.

This means that even if, as I expect, the monthly rate of inflation improves in October, I am leaning toward supporting an increase in our policy rate of 25 basis points at the FOMC's December meeting.

noteSrc.title: Waller, The Economic Outlook and Some Thoughts on Labor Market Dynamism

events.title: FOMC Member Barr Speaks
notes: Today, I will begin by summarizing the current state of economic inequality in the United States, assisted by new results from a long-running survey of households conducted by the Federal Reserve, and then show where this fits into the history of inequality over the past century or so.

Economic growth, technological change, education, and globalization also play key roles. 14 The Evolution of the Labor and Capital Shares of National Income Some of these trends are most clearly seen in the decline in the share of national income going to labor over the past 25 years.

The available evidence from across the globe suggests that advances in digital technology have lowered the price of investment in technology relative to labor. 19 If capital is cheaper relative to labor, firms use relatively more of it.

AI could be what some researchers call capital-biased innovation, in which the returns go primarily to capital rather than to labor. 26 In previous remarks, I have explored scenarios for how AI could evolve as a technology and how it could affect labor markets.

Autor (2025), "Polanyi's Paradox and the Shape of Employment Growth," in Re-Evaluating Labor Market Dynamics: A Symposium Sponsored by the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City (Kansas City: Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City, pp. 129–77).

noteSrc.title: Barr, American Inequality and the Future of AI

events.title: FOMC Member Jefferson Speaks
notes: Next, I will turn to what evidence we have regarding the adoption of artificial intelligence (AI). 2 I will consider how widely these tools are being used, in which sectors, and what recent research tells us about their potential effects on productivity.
Then, I will consider the implications of rapid technological change for the economy more broadly, including for aggregate supply and demand, for inflation, and for the labor market.

That productivity growth was not purely due to investing in more capital; instead, it also reflected increases in what economists call total factor productivity, or TFP. 9 The seeds of the 1990s productivity boom were planted long before Solow's observations in 1987.
Labor productivity growth averaged 2.2 percent between 2020 and 2025, a welcome step up from the modest 1.5 percent average growth rate seen over the previous business cycle.

Over the medium term, the supply of these goods should catch up, and the broader boost to aggregate productivity from adoption should materialize. 19 Both of those developments should ease the upward pressure on prices we see today.

noteSrc.title: Jefferson, New Technology, Old Questions: Productivity Puzzles and the Macroeconomy
